column2: A copper-zinc alloy that looks like gold, invented by the London clockmaker Christopher Pinchbeck in the 1700s. It was so widely used for cheap jewellery that "pinchbeck" came to mean anything fake.
Better known as nitinol: bend it out of shape and it springs back when warmed, because its crystal structure switches between two forms. It's a staple of science videos, and of stents and braces.
Despite the name, it often contains no silver at all: it's usually copper with tin or nickel, and sometimes lead. It's the metal of most cheap "silver" trinkets.

NaK: a mix of two metals that are solid on their own but liquid together at room temperature. Science videos love it for what it does when it meets water, so it's a better-known answer than it sounds.
